source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Across all domains, hours of deliberate practice (DP) explain a modest share of performance differences. Most variance is left to other factors.
numbers: 88 articles, 111 independent samples, 157 effect sizes, N=11,135. Mean r=.35, 95% CI [.30,.39]; 12% of variance (CI 9-15%); 88% unexplained. I2=84.9 (high heterogeneity). 10 of 157 correlations were negative.
quote: deliberate practice ... is not as important as Ericsson and his colleagues have argued
limits: Hours are retrospective self-reports in most studies. Ericsson and Harwell (2019) say the DP definition was too loose; see the Ericsson and Harwell line below.
agent_relevance: A scaffold that just repeats practice cannot expect most of its gain from volume. Treat volume as a minor lever.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Domain is a strong moderator. DP explains a lot in games, music and sports, little in education, and nothing reliable in professions.
numbers: Variance explained: games 26% (r=.51), music 21% (r=.46), sports 18% (r=.42), education 4% (r=.21), professions <1% (r=.05, p=.62). Q(4)=49.09, p<.001. Effect sizes: music 28, sports 60, education 51, professions 7, games 11.
limits: Professions had only 7 effect sizes. Authors suggest DP is less well defined there and that prior knowledge differs between people.
agent_relevance: Our agent works on open-ended tasks. The low end of this table is the relevant one: practice pays least there.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Predictability of the task environment moderates the DP effect, as the authors predicted.
numbers: Variance explained: 24% for high-predictability activities (r=.49), 12% for moderate (r=.35), 4% for low-predictability (r=.21). Q(1)=20.49, b=0.14, T2=.05, p<.001.
limits: Predictability was rated by coders, not measured. It is confounded with domain.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that repetition helps most where the task is stable and repeatable. Open reasoning tasks sit nearer the low end.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: How practice and performance are measured changes the effect size a lot. The log method, probably the most valid, gives the smallest effect.
numbers: Practice measure: interview 20% (r=.45), questionnaire 12% (r=.34), log 5% (r=.22); Q(2)=16.19, p<.001. Performance measure: group membership 26% (r=.51), lab task 14% (r=.37), expert ratings 9% (r=.30), standardized objective score 8% (r=.28); Q(3)=14.41, p=.002.
limits: Retrospective methods may inflate the link through recall bias and knowing the group. The paper calls the log method presumably more valid.
agent_relevance: Self-report studies overstate the effect. Our agent logs real practice, so expect the smaller numbers.

source: Macnamara, Hambrick, Oswald (2014) Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: a meta-analysis
finding: Restricting to solitary DP does not raise the effect. Publication bias checks found no sign of missing null results.
numbers: Solitary-only model (59 effect sizes): 11% overall (games 23, music 23, sports 22, education 3). Excluding team sports (53 effect sizes): 10% (games 23, music 23, sports 28, education 3). Funnel plot roughly symmetric; trim-and-fill found no missing effects.
limits: The sports meta-analysis later found unpublished studies had smaller effects (see Macnamara 2016 lines).
agent_relevance: Low concern about bias in the headline numbers; some concern for the small-k domain splits.

source: Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: a meta-analysis
finding: In sport, DP explains 18% of variance overall but almost none among elite athletes. Skill level is the key moderator.
numbers: 52 independent samples, 63 effect sizes, N=2,765. Overall r=.43, CI [.35,.50], 18% (CI 12-25%). Subelite r=.44, mixed samples r=.54 (29%), elite r=.11, p=.50 (1%; 6 effect sizes, N=228).
quote: deliberate practice accounted for only 1% of the variance in performance among elite-level performers
limits: Elite set is small. Including one effect excluded for r>1 moves elite r from .11 to .28 (8%), still not significant. Range restriction at the top may play a part.
agent_relevance: Volume stops separating the very best. If our agent is already near its ceiling, more practice adds little.

source: Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: a meta-analysis
finding: The sports DP effect is similar across task types but depends on how performance is scored.
numbers: Team 17% vs individual 19%; open 17% vs closed 19%; ball 20% vs non-ball 15%; externally paced 17% vs internally paced 41% (r=.64). Performance by group membership 25%, standardized score 20%, expert ratings 2% (r=.14). Solitary DP only (14 effect sizes, N=488): r=.47, CI [.33,.58], 22%; solitary vs not Q(1)=.25, p=.62.
limits: Internally paced sports have few samples. Judge ratings were weakly related to hours.
agent_relevance: Judge-scored outcomes (closest to LLM-as-judge) showed the weakest link to practice. Use objective scores where possible.

source: Macnamara, Moreau, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between deliberate practice and performance in sports: a meta-analysis
finding: Starting earlier does not make higher-skill athletes better. Unpublished studies show smaller practice effects than published ones.
numbers: Starting age, higher vs lower skill: 0.11 years later (5.6 weeks), CI [-.41,.62], p=.68; 24 effect sizes, N=1,477. Published (38 cases, N=2,066) vs unpublished (25 cases, N=699): unpublished r=.33, CI [.21,.44], 11% of variance; Q(1)=4.23, p=.04. Median N of unpublished studies 46.
limits: Starting-age effect not significant, so small effects cannot be ruled out. Unpublished studies are mostly small.
agent_relevance: Early exposure is not a proxy for later skill. Do not over-weight the order of an early curriculum.

source: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Deliberate practice: Is that all it takes to become an expert?
finding: Reanalysis of chess studies, corrected for unreliability: DP explains about a third of reliable variance.
numbers: Chess: average 34% of variance (avg corrected r=.57; sample-size-weighted .49), 66% unexplained. Sensitivity: even if DP reliability is only .60, 54.7% stays unexplained; reliability .90 gives 30.2% explained. Charness et al. (2005): Study 1 r=.54 (N=200), Study 2 r=.48 (N=164).
limits: Corrections assume DP reliability .80 and chess rating reliability .91. Authors asked Ericsson's group for the 1993 raw data; it was not available. Bilali et al. N=57 gave r=.90, a small sample.
agent_relevance: Gives a middle estimate (about a third) for a rule-bound, feedback-rich domain.

source: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Deliberate practice: Is that all it takes to become an expert?
finding: Same reanalysis for music: DP explains about 30% of reliable variance.
numbers: Music: average 29.9% (avg corrected r=.52; sample-weighted .52), 70.1% unexplained. Range 26.3% (reliability .90) to 39.6% (reliability .60). Ruthsatz et al. (2008) Study 2B N=19, r^=.68 CI [.14,1.0]; Study 2A N=64, r^=.39 CI [.09,.65].
limits: Studies use different performance measures. Platz et al. (2014) dispute the use of variance shares.
agent_relevance: A music figure near 30% can be used as a planning value for practice-heavy domains.

source: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Deliberate practice: Is that all it takes to become an expert?
finding: In chess, DP totals overlap heavily across skill groups; some masters had less practice than the mean of lower groups.
numbers: Masters ranged 832 to 24,284 h (almost three orders of magnitude). Of 16 masters, 5 (31.3%) had less DP than the expert-group mean and 2 (12.5%) less than the intermediate mean. Of 31 intermediates, 8 (25.8%) had more DP than the expert mean and 4 (12.9%) more than the master mean. Polgar sisters: peak rating 2735 after about 59,904 h vs 2577 after about 79,248 h.
limits: Hours are self-estimates. The Polgar figures come from a case study (Howard 2011) based on biographical accounts.
agent_relevance: Strong individual differences in learning rate. A fixed practice budget will not give uniform gains across models or tasks.

source: Hambrick, Oswald, Altmann, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Deliberate practice: Is that all it takes to become an expert?
finding: Working memory capacity adds to DP in predicting skill and does not simply reflect practice.
numbers: Meinz and Hambrick (2010), pianists' sight-reading: DP explained 45.1% of variance; working memory capacity added 7.4% (significant). Working memory and DP correlated r=.003. No DP x working-memory interaction, so working memory mattered as much at high DP.
limits: Ericsson argues working memory capacity is partly an acquired skill. One highly dynamic task.
agent_relevance: Base capacity (model size, context) is a separate limit that practice or scaffolds do not remove.

source: Hambrick, Altmann, Oswald, Meinz, Gobet (2014) Facing facts about deliberate practice
finding: Reply to the Platz et al. critique. They hold that DP is important but explains only part of the variance, and defend reporting r-squared.
numbers: Their estimate: DP explained about 30% of music variance. Platz et al. rc=.61 (36% of variance). They cite a Kopiez co-authored study (Jabusch et al. 2009) where life practice 'predicted only 17% of variance'.
quote: our conclusion is not that deliberate practice is unimportant ... it is that deliberate practice is not as important as Ericsson and colleagues have argued
limits: Rebuttal piece with no new data. The r versus r-squared disagreement is about framing.
agent_relevance: Report both r and variance when judging whether a practice-like step is worth its cost.

source: Platz, Kopiez, Lehmann, Wolf (2014) The influence of deliberate practice on musical achievement: a meta-analysis
finding: A rival music meta-analysis restricted to task-specific practice and objective scores finds a larger effect.
numbers: 13 studies, N=788. Corrected aggregate rc=0.61, 95% CI [0.54,0.67]. Q(12)=8.19, p=.77, I2=0%. 81.2% of variance across studies was artefact. Four studies carry 50% of the weight.
limits: Hunter-Schmidt correction for unreliability can inflate. Narrow study selection. They argue r, not r-squared, should be interpreted. Includes practice that 'by definition includes DP'.
agent_relevance: The size of the DP effect depends on definition and correction. For music the plausible range is 21% to 36% of variance.

source: Macnamara and Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer (1993)
finding: A preregistered, double-blind, results-blind replication of the 1993 violinist study did not reproduce the core finding. The best violinists had not practised more than the good ones.
numbers: Cleveland Institute of Music, 13 best, 13 good, 13 less accomplished (N=39). Accumulated practice alone to age 18: best M=8,224 h, good M=9,844, less accomplished 4,558. Best vs good t24=-0.93, p=.364, d=-0.38. Group effect eta2=.26 (original: 48% of variance). Good vs less accomplished d=1.33, p=.005. By age 20 both top groups had over 10,000 h.
quote: We did not replicate the core finding that accumulated amounts of deliberate practice corresponded to each skill level.
limits: Original had 10 per group at the Berlin academy. Group assignment by faculty nomination. Retrospective estimates. The replication authors note their violinists may be more elite (best group averaged 13.31 competitions, original students 1.23 overall).
agent_relevance: A failed direct replication of the founding result. Treat the 'complete correspondence' claim as unreliable.

source: Macnamara and Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer (1993)
finding: Current weekly practice: the best violinists reported less solitary practice than the good group. Teacher-designed practice, the theoretical definition, did no better than practice alone.
numbers: Weekly practice alone: best M=22.69 h, good 30.65, less accomplished 9.58 (best vs good p=.024, d=-1.03). Teacher-designed weekly: best 10.23, good 14.88, less 4.46; group effect not significant (chi2=3.14, p=.208). Accumulated teacher-designed practice to 18: best 6,251 h vs good 6,821 (d=-0.15). The two accumulated measures correlate r=.72.
limits: N=39, one instrument, retrospective estimates.
agent_relevance: Quality-of-practice claims need direct measurement. Hours of teacher-designed practice added no explanatory power.

source: Macnamara and Maitra (2019) The role of deliberate practice in expert performance: revisiting Ericsson, Krampe and Tesch-Romer (1993)
finding: Practice estimates were biased upward but not by group, and the replication effect matches the meta-analytic average, not the original.
numbers: Weekly estimates exceeded diary logs (F1,35=19.62, p<.001, partial eta2=.36), with no group difference (F2,35=1.45, p=.249). Replication 26% of variance vs original 48% vs music meta-analytic average 23%. Original study compared 10 per group; accumulated hours in original: best 7,410, good 5,301, less accomplished 3,420.
limits: Single replication; may differ from 1993 in skill level.
agent_relevance: Small extreme-group designs overstate effects. Be suspicious of single small-N gains when evaluating scaffold changes.

source: Mosing, Madison, Pedersen, Kuja-Halkola, Ullen (2014) Practice does not make perfect: no causal effect of music practice on music ability
finding: Large twin study: practice and ability are linked mostly through shared genes. Identical twins who differ in practice did not differ in ability.
numbers: 10,500 Swedish twins. Practice-ability associations rs=.18 to .36. Practice heritable 40% to 70%. No ability difference within monozygotic pairs that differed in practice; nonshared environment did not contribute.
limits: Only the abstract was read (via Europe PMC). Ability is a discrimination test, not performance. Practice is self-reported. Adults, cross-sectional.
agent_relevance: Practice and ability can share a common cause. The same confound arises if an agent practises more because it is already better.

source: Mosing, Verweij, Hambrick, Pedersen, Ullen (2024) Testing the deliberate practice theory: does practice reduce the heritability of musical expertise?
finding: A direct test of a DP prediction: genetic effects should shrink with more practice. They did not. Heritability rose with practice.
numbers: 6,471 twins (1,302 complete pairs), mean age 40.7. About 50% of expertise differences genetic, about 25% shared environment, about 25% residual. Variance fell with practice because shared-environment and residual variance fell; genetic variance was unchanged. Phenotypic practice-ability r=.36. Players vs non-players d=0.77 (men), 0.78 (women).
limits: Ability is a discrimination test (pitch, melody, rhythm), not performance. Practice reported in range categories. Swedish adults only.
agent_relevance: Practice equalises the environment but leaves underlying differences. A discriminating prediction of DP theory failed.

source: Mosing et al. (2021) Why is an early start of training related to musical skills in adulthood? A genetically informative study
finding: Early start is linked to adult skill mostly through lifetime practice hours and family factors, with little support for a sensitive period.
numbers: 310 professional musicians and 7,786 twins. After adjusting for practice, onset age predicted only pitch discrimination (beta=-0.07 in musicians, -0.30 in twins; p<.001), not rhythm (beta=-0.03, p=.69; -0.02, p=.09). Achievement p>.14. Twin analyses: the link with aptitude fully explained by familial factors.
limits: Cross-sectional, self-reported onset and practice.
agent_relevance: Counters the idea that early exposure raises the ceiling. No case for front-loading curriculum in the scaffold.

source: Hambrick, Macnamara, Oswald (2020) Is the deliberate practice view defensible? A review of evidence and discussion of issues
finding: Documents shifting definitions of DP over 25 years, making the theory hard to test. Says Ericsson's own reanalysis used looser criteria than he applied to the 2014 meta-analysis.
numbers: Ericsson (2014) rejected 87 of the 88 studies as not DP. Ericsson and Harwell (2019) kept 14 of 88 (8 effects coded DP, 6 purposeful); 7 of the 8 DP effects came from studies Ericsson had rejected. Their corrected mean r rose from .54 to .78 (61% of reliable variance).
limits: Written by authors of the 2014 meta-analysis, an interested party. Argues for a multifactorial model and open science.
agent_relevance: A framework with a movable definition cannot be falsified. State a measurable test up front for each schema claim.

source: Ericsson and Harwell (2019) Deliberate practice and proposed limits on the effects of practice on the acquisition of expert performance: why the original definition matters
finding: Rival reanalysis: restricting to the original definition (individualised, teacher-guided, purposeful) gives larger effects. They also argue genetic accounts have explained little.
numbers: Reanalysis of 14 of the 88 studies in Macnamara et al. (2014): practice explained 29% of variance (61% after attenuation correction; r=.54 to .78). They quote the 2014 estimate as 14% for what they call structured practice.
quote: Their definition of deliberate practice differs significantly from the original definition
limits: Self-selected study set; teacher criterion loosened compared with Ericsson (2014), per Hambrick et al. (2020). Correction widens confidence intervals. Full text read up to the abstract and introduction only.
agent_relevance: Competing explanation: quality, not hours. For an agent this maps to targeted feedback loops versus raw repetition.

source: Burgoyne, Sala, Gobet, Macnamara, Campitelli, Hambrick (2016) The relationship between cognitive ability and chess skill: a comprehensive meta-analysis
finding: Cognitive ability predicts chess skill, more so in youth and at lower skill. The link fades for adult ranked players.
numbers: 19 studies, 26 independent samples. Mean r=.24, CI [.18,.30]. Gf .24, Gc .22, Gsm .25, Gs .24. Gf: youth r=.32 vs adult r=.11 (CI [-.01,.22], p=.071); unranked .32 vs ranked .14 (CI [.02,.25]). Numerical .35, verbal .19, visuospatial .13.
limits: Correlational. Range restriction among strong players. Chess only.
agent_relevance: Base ability matters early and domain knowledge dominates later, like model capacity versus task knowledge.

source: Campitelli and Gobet (2011) Deliberate practice: necessary but not sufficient (APS press release summary)
finding: Chess: a floor of practice is needed but no amount guarantees mastery. Other factors named: IQ in children, handedness, working memory.
numbers: Argentine chess players: about 3,000 h at the fastest to master; some masters needed about 30,000 h; some played over 30,000 h without reaching master. About 82% of adult chess players are right-handed vs about 90% of the general population.
quote: there are even people that practiced more than 30,000 hours and didn't achieve this
limits: Secondary source (press release). Journal text not opened (HTTP 403). Hours are self-estimates. Sample size not stated there.
agent_relevance: Necessary but not sufficient: a minimum of targeted work, then variable returns.

source: Sala and Gobet (2017) Does far transfer exist? Negative evidence from chess, music, and working memory training
finding: Practice in one skill rarely transfers to other abilities. Effects vanish with active control groups.
numbers: Music instruction on cognitive/academic outcomes: 0.25 SD CI [0.17,0.34] (k=64) vs passive controls, 0.03 SD CI [-0.07,0.12] (k=54) vs active controls. Working-memory training: 0.18 SD CI [-0.09,0.26] (k=34) passive, 0.05 SD CI [-0.05,0.15] (k=40) active. Chess: one active-control study, 0.10 SD. Chess overall: mathematics 0.20 CI [0.03,0.36], literacy 0.11 CI [0.00,0.22].
quote: The size of the effects was inversely related to the quality of the experimental design.
limits: Children's cognitive and academic outcomes only. Chess pooled figures cover mostly passive-control studies.
agent_relevance: A scaffold tuned on one task family should not be expected to lift other families. Test against active-control baselines.

source: Barth, Guellich, Macnamara, Hambrick (2022) Predictors of junior versus senior elite performance are opposite: a systematic review and meta-analysis of participation patterns
finding: Predictors of junior success are the opposite of predictors of adult world-class success. Focused early practice helps juniors; world-class adults had more varied practice and later specialisation.
numbers: 71 reports, 262 samples, 685 effect sizes, N=9,241. Adult world-class vs national-class: more childhood multi-sport coach-led practice, later main-sport start, less main-sport practice, slower initial progress (|d| 0.23 to 0.50, all p<.001). Juniors: earlier start, more main-sport practice, faster progress (|d| 0.23 to 0.61). Peer-led play negligible. GRADE moderate to high for most predictors.
limits: Only the abstract was read (via Europe PMC). Correlational with survivor effects. Sports only.
agent_relevance: Early gains from focused practice can mislead about the long-run ceiling. Check scaffold changes on later-stage held-out tasks, not only early gains.

source: Hambrick, Altmann, Oswald, Meinz, Gobet, Campitelli (2014) Accounting for expert performance: the devil is in the details (reply to Ericsson 2014)
finding: Reply to Ericsson's defence of DP (Ericsson 2014, Intelligence 45:81-103, arguing expert performance cannot be extrapolated from general-population samples). The authors say his defence has contradictions and errors and restate their partial-explanation finding.
numbers: No new numbers. A companion reply, 'It might happen in the very beginning' (pp. 107-108), argues lifespan studies need novice samples.
limits: Only the repository record and search snippets were read, not the paper. Not independent verification.
agent_relevance: Shows where the dispute lies: definition, range restriction, and sampling. A checklist for judging our own claims.
